title: 道德經 第四十章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 40, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 72. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 40 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 去用 (Dispensing with Use). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: to turn back, to go the way one came, to come round again (later written 返)
the one that — nominalising what precedes: 'what turns back'
the Way
the genitive particle: 's, of — not the object pronoun here
movement, the making of a move

sentences.l: What turns back — the Way's moving;
sentences.i: Turning back is how the Way moves;
sentences.n:
There is no verb in this line at all. 反者, 'what turns back', and 道之動, 'the Way's moving', are set down side by side, and the bare juxtaposition is the equation; Classical Chinese has no word for 'is'. English must insert one, which is why the literal line puts a dash where the Chinese puts nothing.

反 is not opposition and not 'the opposite'. It is going back the way you came — the word later written 返, 'to return' — and it names the motion this book keeps describing: the full emptying, the high resting on the low, the extreme turning into what it was not. Wang Bi glosses the line by pointing straight back at the chapter you have just read: the high takes the low as its footing, the honoured takes the base as its root, what-is takes what-is-not as its use — this, he says, is its turning back.

Watch 之. Here it is the plain genitive, 'the Way's'. In chapter 38's 莫之應 the same character was an object pronoun standing in front of its verb. It does both jobs constantly and only position tells you which.

morph.gloss: weak — here what is soft, pliant and unresisting
the one that — 'what is weak'
the Way
genitive: 's, of
use, the putting to work, what a thing is good for

sentences.l: What is weak — the Way's use.
sentences.i: Weakness is how the Way does its work.
sentences.n:
The matching half of the couplet, and it still rhymes: 動 dòng and 用 yòng rhymed in Old Chinese and rhyme in Mandarin, so this pair can be heard as verse without anyone's say-so. Two five-character lines, identical in shape, differing in two places — this is the book's basic unit of thought.

弱 is 'weak' in the flat dictionary sense, but what the book means by it is the soft and unresisting: the water and the newborn of the later chapters. 用 is use, function, what a thing is good for — chapter 11 built a whole argument on it, that the hollow of a bowl is its 用, not the clay. So: turning back is how the Way moves, and being weak is how it works. Between them the two lines state the mechanics of the entire book.

sentences.t:
天下萬物生於有，
有生於無。

morph.gloss: all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it
heaven, sky
below, under
the ten-thousand things — everything there is
ten thousand; countless
thing, creature
to be born, to come to life
the all-purpose preposition, standing after its verb — here 'from, out of'
to have, there is — here as a noun: what-is, being
what-is, being
to be born
from
to lack, there is not — here as a noun: what-is-not, nothing

sentences.l:
The ten-thousand things of all-under-heaven are born from what-is;
what-is is born from what-is-not.
sentences.i: The ten thousand things under heaven are born out of what there is; and what there is, out of what there is not.
sentences.n:
有 and 無 are ordinary verbs — 'there is' and 'there is not' — pressed here into service as nouns, and English has to invent a shape for them: what-is and what-is-not, being and nothing. That parts of speech move like this is not a difficulty in the text but the grammar of the language; nothing marks the shift except position.

於 stands after the verb it belongs to, not before it — the reverse of English — and covers whatever relation the sense needs — at, in, to, than, and here from.

This is where the chapter's halves join. If the Way's motion is turning back, then the direction of birth is also the direction of return, and what everything comes out of is the thing with nothing in it.

Chapter 40 is among the material found on the Guodian bamboo slips of about 300 BC, and the slips' version of this last line is shorter than the received one. On the usual reconstruction it has the things of the world born from what-is and from what-is-not side by side, rather than in a chain running things ← being ← nothing. The difference is genuine and much argued; the text here is the received one, and the chain is what it says.
